anchor: My love is as a fever
title: Sonnet 147 and the 'dark lady'
short: This is one of the late sonnets (127-152) addressed to or about a dark woman. Here love is a fever the lover wants to keep alive.
body: The poem develops a single medical conceit: love is a disease, and reason is the doctor who gives up the case. It follows Sonnet 146, the soul's address to the body, and some readers connect the two through the idea of feeding (146 ends 'And death once dead, there's no more dying then'). 'Still' means always: the fever keeps longing for what feeds it. These sonnets are often called the 'dark lady' sonnets, but the label is the critics', not Shakespeare's.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: nurseth
short: 'Nurse' means nourish or foster. He longs for what feeds the disease and makes it last, just as fevered patients crave harmful food.
body: Galenic medicine taught that a sick appetite craves what harms it, and that giving in to it 'feeds' the illness. 'Nurse' can mean either to heal or to keep alive, and Shakespeare uses both: what nurses this fever is no cure. Line 3 repeats the idea with 'preserve the ill'. The paradox of a sick man who wants to stay sick is the core of the poem, and the first quatrain states it three times over.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

anchor: The uncertain sickly appetite to please
title: appetite
short: The aim is to please an unstable, diseased appetite. 'Appetite' means both hunger and sexual desire.
body: 'Uncertain' means fickle and changeable, as a fever's cravings are. The inverted word order ('the ... appetite to please') holds back the verb. Renaissance writers on melancholy and love-sickness treat erotic desire as a disorder of the appetite; Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) later gathered that tradition together. The quatrain is one long sentence. Its subject is the fever of l. 1, which feeds on the very thing that keeps the illness going.

sources.cite: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Part 3, 'Love-Melancholy'

title: Reason the physician
short: Reason, which should govern passion, is the doctor. Angry that his advice is ignored, he leaves the patient.
body: In Renaissance psychology reason was meant to rule the appetites, and moralists often called it the soul's physician. Here the doctor is 'Angry' because his 'prescriptions' (orders, regimen) are not 'kept' (obeyed). Like a real doctor dropping a hopeless case, he walks out and leaves the patient to his delirium. The physician's anger is a comic touch in a grim poem.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: approve
short: 'Approve' means prove by experience. In despair he now finds out that desire is death.
body: The older sense of 'approve' (from Latin approbare, to prove) is to show or learn by trial, not to give consent. 'Desperate' means without hope, and it also carries the theological sense of despair, the sin of refusing to trust in God's mercy. So the line describes a man who learns the truth only after it is too late to act on it. The theological echo matters, because the sonnet that precedes it is about the soul's salvation.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: Desire is death ... except
short: Probably: he now learns that desire is fatal, which medicine forbade (took exception to). The syntax allows several readings.
body: 'Physic' is medicine, and 'except' most likely means object to or forbid. So medicine forbade the desire that he now finds to be death. Some editors take 'which' to refer to death, which physic kept away as long as he obeyed it. 'Death' may also carry the period's sexual sense of orgasm, and many readers think the 'disease' is venereal. Compare Romans 6:23 ('the wages of sin is death') and James 1:15, where lust gives birth to sin and sin to death.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary

title: Past cure, past care
short: He reverses the proverb 'past cure, past care': his reason has stopped caring, so he can no longer be cured.
body: Shakespeare uses the proverb elsewhere: 'Things past redress are now with me past care' (Richard II 2.3) and 'past cure is still past care' (Love's Labour's Lost 5.2). Here he reverses its order: because Reason is past caring, the patient is past cure. The chiasmus of 'cure ... care' makes the sound of the proverb part of the argument. 'Reason' is now capitalized in the archive, marking the faculty as a character in the little drama.

sources.cite: M. P. Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1950), s.v. 'past cure, past care'
Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: frantic-mad
short: 'Frantic' means delirious or raving (from Greek phrenitis, inflammation of the brain). The fever has become madness.
body: In ancient and Renaissance medicine phrenitis was a fever with delirium, so 'frantic-mad' completes the medical picture. 'Evermore unrest' means endless restlessness. Lines 11-12 list the symptoms: both thought and speech run 'At random from the truth', 'vainly' (uselessly, falsely) expressed. The words 'unrest' and 'random' push the poem from medical description into the language of madness. The patient has lost both health and sense.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary

title: discourse
short: 'Discourse' means both speech and the power of reasoning (the 'discourse of reason'). Both are now like a madman's.
body: Compare Hamlet's 'a beast that wants discourse of reason' (1.2). 'Random' in the next line (Quarto 'randon') meant headlong or impetuous, from Old French randon, the rush of a gallop. So his very reasoning has become a symptom. The quatrain prepares for the couplet, which gives the clearest example of his false speech: his praise of the lady. The confession that his words have been 'vainly express'd' also casts doubt on the earlier sonnets in her praise.

anchor: For I have sworn thee fair
title: The couplet
short: The couplet proves his madness. He swore she was fair and bright, but she is black as hell, in body and in morals.
body: 'Fair' and 'bright' mean light-skinned and also beautiful or good. 'Black' and 'dark' likewise have both a physical and a moral sense. Sonnet 127 had praised blackness as the new beauty; here it becomes damnation. Critics have noted how violent the couplet is. Some read it as the height of the speaker's disgust with himself; others point out that the excuse of delirium does not soften the insult. 'Black as hell' and 'dark as night' are proverbial similes.

sources.cite: Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 1997; rev. 2010), commentary
Helen Vendler, The Art of Shakespeare's Sonnets (Harvard, 1997), on Sonnet 147
Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale, 1977), commentary
